text:
Most data scientist loops run four kinds of round. Probability and statistics questions. A modeling case: how would you predict this? An experiment to design, usually an A B test. And a coding screen, in Python and pandas or in SQL.

Across all four, interviewers score the same five things. Statistics and probability: distributions, tests and intervals. Modeling: the bias and variance trade-off, regularization, validation, and the metric you pick. Experimentation: the design, its power, and the pitfalls. Coding, in pandas, NumPy and SQL. And communication: explaining a model and its caveats to someone who doesn't build them.

AI, artificial intelligence, has brought in new questions. Evaluating a feature built on a large language model, an LLM, is now treated as a measurement problem: an eval set, a confidence interval on its pass rate, and a check that an LLM judge agrees with experts. Experiments on AI features, where the output changes from one run to the next. Checking code or an analysis an assistant wrote. And some rounds allow an assistant while others ban it, so ask the recruiter which is which.

The series runs in the track's order: eleven videos, from statistics to LLM evaluation, and a hundred and fifty-eight questions. Machine learning and experimentation each get two videos. In every one, the questions worth a figure come first, and the one-line answers close it. Each page carries practice too: concept checks, challenges that run in your browser, and a hundred and ten multiple-choice questions across the whole track. Most loops open with probability and statistics questions, and so does this series. Next: Statistics.
